processing: A pan-fired green: fresh leaf is spread, fixed at 180–220°C, rolled, broken up, dried in stages, then finished for aroma and graded.
harvest_season: Exact picking dates are little documented; as with other Yunnan greens, spring leaf is usually the most prized.
appearance_dry: Tight, even strands with some tender stem, in a slightly greyish, glossy green.
taste_profile: Clean, high aroma with a strong, mellow body.

brewing.notes: Large-leaf green has more grip than eastern greens, so go easy on leaf and time.

vintage_note: Usually sold as the current year's tea, as with other Chinese greens, and best drunk within about a year. Local names on the market have included Bai Zhu Yin Hao and Yunwu teas, so look for the appellation and the picking date.
description:
Baizhushan Tea is a protected green tea from Fabiao Town in Shuangbai County, in Yunnan's Chuxiong prefecture. In a province known for pu-erh and Dian Hong, it is something different: a high-mountain green made from large-leaf plants.

The gardens sit at 2,000 metres or more, with heavy mist and a wide swing between day and night temperatures. The leaf is pan-fired hot, then rolled and dried in stages, with the aim of keeping the leaf, liquor and spent leaves all green with no red stems.

The cup is bright yellow-green with a high, clean aroma and more weight than a Zhejiang green. Because large leaf can bite, use a bit less tea and water just off the boil, and keep the first steep short.

The protected zone covers 13 villages in Fabiao, so the name is a real place claim. Ask for the picking date and treat it as a fresh tea: seal it and drink it within the year.
history:
According to local records, people from Fabiao brought Yunnan large-leaf tea from Jingdong County in 1942 and planted it successfully on Baizhu Mountain. The Shuangbai county gazetteer mentions scattered tea in the Ming and Qing periods at Ejia, and a 1958 push by the Fabiao commune, which sent young workers to open gardens on the mountain.

China's Ministry of Agriculture registered Baizhushan Tea as a geographical indication on 15 April 2013.
